advisory.title: Unbounded response body buffering in Streamable HTTP clients
advisory.description:
Before 3.9.0, the built-in Streamable HTTP clients in rmcp read non-streaming
HTTP response bodies into memory with no size limit. Both the reqwest client
(`transport-streamable-http-client-reqwest`) and the Unix socket client
(`transport-streamable-http-client-unix-socket`) were affected:

- `application/json` responses to POST requests were read in full before
  parsing.
- Non-2xx responses were read in full for error reporting.

A malicious or compromised MCP server can answer with a body that never ends,
for example a chunked `application/json` response that streams whitespace. The
client buffers it until the process runs out of memory. This works during
`initialize`, before any authentication. On desktop or agent hosts, this
terminates the whole host application.

Server-sent event streams are not affected. Each event is already capped by
`max_sse_event_size`, and events are not accumulated.

The flaw was corrected in 3.9.0. Successful JSON bodies are limited to 16 MiB
and non-success bodies to 64 KiB. Bytes are counted while streaming, after
decompression. An oversized `Content-Length` is rejected before the body is
read, and an oversized body is rejected with
`StreamableHttpError::ResponseBodyTooLarge` instead of being truncated.

If you cannot upgrade, use a custom `StreamableHttpClient` that enforces a
response body limit, or connect only to trusted MCP servers.

advisory.title: OAuth client SSRF filter checks host strings, not resolved addresses
advisory.description:
From 2.0.0 until 3.7.0, the rmcp OAuth client decided whether it may fetch an
authorization server's metadata URL by inspecting only the host string. It
rejected literal loopback, private and link-local IP addresses and known cloud
metadata hostnames, but it did not resolve other hostnames. A hostname that
resolves to an internal address passed the check.

A malicious MCP server can return protected-resource metadata that names an
authorization server whose hostname resolves to an internal address. The client
then sends GET requests to that address during discovery.

The same release fixes two related bypasses:

- Bracketed IPv6 literals such as `http://[::1]:6379/` were not recognized as
  internal, because the check kept the brackets from the URL host.
- `token_endpoint` and `registration_endpoint` from authorization server
  metadata were not checked at all, and token requests follow redirects. A
  malicious authorization server could make the client send POST requests to
  an internal address.

The impact is client-side SSRF. Responses are not returned to the attacker
directly. Unauthenticated internal HTTP services are reachable. Cloud metadata
endpoints that require headers or IMDSv2 are largely unaffected.

The flaw was corrected in 3.7.0. `AuthorizationManager::new` now builds its HTTP
client with a DNS resolver that applies the address policy to every resolved
address, and checks every IP-literal URL and followed redirect against the same
policy. Loopback and private addresses are allowed only when the MCP server's
own URL names one of that class. Deployments that reach their authorization
server through a hostname that resolves to a private address should use
`AuthorizationManager::new_allowing_private_addresses`.

Clients supplied through `new_with_oauth_http_client` are not covered by the
resolved-address checks. Such clients must enforce their own outbound address
policy.

advisory.title: Unbounded tool schema cache in Streamable HTTP server transport
advisory.description:
From 3.0.0 until 3.6.0, `StreamableHttpService` cached the result of
`ServerHandler::get_tool` in a process-wide map keyed by the tool name of
incoming `tools/call` requests. The map had no size limit and no eviction, and
it also cached unknown tool names.

An entry was added while the request headers were validated, before the request
could be rejected, so requests answered with HTTP 400 still grew the map. A
client that can reach the endpoint can send `tools/call` requests with distinct
tool names, each up to the default 4 MiB body limit, until the server runs out
of memory. rmcp does not authenticate requests itself, so servers without an
authentication layer in front of the endpoint are exposed to unauthenticated
clients.

Only servers that use the Streamable HTTP server transport and receive requests
at protocol version `2026-07-28` or later are affected.

The flaw was corrected in 3.6.0 by removing the cache. The transport now calls
`ServerHandler::get_tool` on each request.

If you cannot upgrade, put authentication in front of the endpoint, or reject
`tools/call` requests for unknown tool names before they reach
`StreamableHttpService`.

advisory.title: DNS rebinding vulnerability in rmcp Streamable HTTP server transport
advisory.description:
Prior to version 1.4.0, the `rmcp` crate's Streamable HTTP server transport did
not validate the incoming `Host` header.

This allowed a malicious public website, via a DNS rebinding attack, to send
requests to an MCP server running on the victim's loopback or private-network
interface.

An attacker who convinced a victim to visit a malicious page could enumerate and
invoke tools exposed by a locally running rmcp-based MCP server, read resources
and prompts, and trigger side effects limited by the tools exposed by that
server.

Non-HTTP transports such as stdio and child-process transports are not affected.

## Patches

The issue was fixed in `rmcp` 1.4.0 by adding default loopback-only host
allowlist validation for the Streamable HTTP server transport. Incoming HTTP
requests now validate the `Host` header and return HTTP 403 when the host is not
allowed.

Users should upgrade to `rmcp >= 1.4.0`.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not possible, place the MCP server behind a reverse proxy
configured to reject requests whose `Host` header is not one of the expected
hostnames. Do not bind the MCP server to `0.0.0.0` without such validation.
